title: Motional refocusing for trap-off Rydberg gates
authors: Yoav Sagi, Ofer Firstenberg, Nir Davidson, Guy Raz
abstract: Rydberg entangling gates in optical-tweezer arrays are commonly executed with the trapping light switched off, so every gate contains a release--and--recapture cycle that heats the atomic motion and can ultimately limit circuit depth. We develop a motional refocusing protocol that exactly removes this heating in the harmonic approximation using only programmable intensity switching of the trapping light. The protocol closes the release--and--recapture cycle for every matched harmonic mode, returning arbitrary motional populations and coherences exactly up to ordinary evolution under the static trap. We derive the recovery sequence in closed form for arbitrary catch depth and prove that, within the experimentally relevant regime, it is the unique globally time-optimal solution under bounded trap intensity. The harmonic theory is then extended in two directions. First, we construct exact common-intensity recovery sequences that simultaneously refocus several nondegenerate harmonic modes, including radial--axial and fully anisotropic three-dimensional traps. Second, we derive a composite sequence that suppresses the leading anharmonic correction of weakly anharmonic traps by canceling all first-order motional transitions induced by the quartic anharmonicity, changing the residual heating law from $U_0^{-2}$ to $U_0^{-4}$. Wave-packet simulations in realistic Gaussian tweezers validate the analytic theory and quantify the residual effects of anharmonicity, finite switching ramps, trap ellipticity, and control errors. Applied to representative cesium Rydberg gates, the protocol suppresses the dominant recapture heating to the anharmonic floor and prevents the associated motional Doppler contribution from increasing with circuit depth. The resulting framework provides a practical route toward heating-free trap-off neutral-atom gates using only trap-intensity modulation.
summary: The paper presents a novel motional refocusing protocol that eliminates heating during the release-and-recapture cycle inherent to Rydberg gates. By precisely controlling the trapping light intensity, the authors restore the atomic motion to its initial state, enabling deeper and more reliable quantum circuits in optical tweezers.
main_problem: Rydberg entangling gates suffer from motional heating due to the release-and-recapture cycle when trapping light is switched off, limiting circuit depth.
main_result: A motional refocusing protocol using only programmable trap intensity switching can exactly remove this heating in the harmonic approximation and suppress leading anharmonic corrections.
method: The authors developed a time-optimal control sequence by promoting classical phase-space refocusing conditions to an exact quantum statement, analyzed via the Ermakov equation.
model_or_system: The system involves neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezers executing Rydberg blockade gates. The dynamics are modeled using a three-dimensional harmonic potential whose evolution is governed by programmable trap intensity switching.
key_observables: Motional populations and coherences, heating ($\Delta ar{n}_{	ext{sud}}$), recapture probability ($P_{1d}(t)$).
important_parameters: Trap frequencies ($\omega_i$), catch depth ($\Lambda$), gate duration ($T$), anharmonicity strength.
main_assumptions: Initial analysis assumes the harmonic approximation; later extensions consider finite ramps and anharmonic corrections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase-space dynamics (echo protocol) and show 1D recapture probabilities comparing quantum vs. classical predictions at various temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper first develops the refocusing protocol in the harmonic approximation, proving its time-optimality. It then extends this theory to multiple modes and incorporates anharmonic corrections by deriving composite sequences. Finally, wave-packet simulations validate the analytic results for realistic Gaussian tweezers.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical, theoretically rigorous method (intensity modulation) to overcome fundamental decoherence/heating limits in neutral atom quantum computing architectures.
